newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's monetary base may overshoot on year.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's monetary base may overshoot on year.

text.p: Mexico's monetary base, which has exploded recently because of the Christmas season, could stay high and overshoot the central bank's year-end target as the economy continues to recovery strongly, economists said.
Normally the demand for money shoots up sharply at this time of the year, but economists say that the economic recovery may push the the monetary base even higher than expected.

"They might overshoot their original expectations for the end of the year due to the fact that the economic recovery has been more pronounced than expected this year," said Ann Ginsburg, economist for Valores Finamex.

Mexico aims to cut inflation by limiting growth in the supply of money, believing that more money in the system means more inflation. The most basic measure is the monetary base, mainly coins and bills in circulation.
The central bank calculates the amount it can grow taking into account growth in the economy, inflation and how much cash people decide to hold.
"Economic growth has been higher and that allows the monetary base to be slightly higher," said ING Barings economist Sergio Martin.
"It could be over by one to two billion pesos more," he said. Other economists say the overshoot could be even higher.

As of Monday, the monetary base was 84.62 billion pesos, but economists say it can vary day by day before the end of the year. Normally the monetary base rises sharply in the first three weeks of December and then declines as extra spending falls.
At most the monetary base was forecast to rise to 84.81 billion for the year, taking into account the expectation of an increase of 18.0 billion pesos in 1996.

The economy has grown more strongly than expected during 1996. Initially, the government's forecast was for growth of about 3.0 percent, but now economists are expecting a rebound of at least 4.5 percent. Inflation, forecast at 20.5 percent by the government, is likely to hit 26 or 27 percent this year.

If that better-than-expected growth continued into the new year, and created greater-than-expected demand for money, then the central bank would be forced to tighten the money supply, economists said. "It is a whole lot different when you overshoot in the last week of the year than in the first quarter of the year," said Bankers Trust economist Robert Gay. "If it continues for a quarter, they can't let it pass by."

The central bank caused some confusion this year over what number observers should use when seeking to assess its year-end base money target, because it gave mixed signals over where the monetary base ended last year.

It had originally thought the monetary base would end 1995 at 63.0 billion pesos. As it turned out the monetary base ended the year at 66.81 billion pesos, before quickly falling during the first part of this year.

Many observers were unsure which number to use as the base for calculating the targetted 18 billion peso growth for this year. The central bank, saying it learned from last year's confusion, declined to give a 1996 year-end figure when it released its 1997 monetary program earlier this month.
The central bank has said that it could be "reasonably close" to its target for the year, but added that unplanned for price and wage increases in December could push up inflation.
